milestones.notes: npm has shipped bundled with the Node.js installer/tarball since the 0.6.x/0.8.x era
net/dgram/dns supported IPv6 from very early Node; not a per-major milestone worth tracking closely
official x64 Windows .msi/tarball added around 0.10; 0.8 was x86-only
reliable with the OpenSSL 1.0.2 bump at Node 4; present but flaky under 0.10/0.12's OpenSSL 1.0.1
node:http2 added experimental behind --expose-http2 in 8.4.0, no flag needed from 8.8.0, marked stable in 10.10.0/10.13.0

ES modules usable behind --experimental-modules with .mjs from 8.5.0; flag no longer required from 12.17.0; package.json "type" field and .cjs/.mjs resolution settled by 13-14; require(esm) for synchronous CJS->ESM interop unflagged in 22.12.0/23
worker_threads unflagged/stable in 12.11.0 -- first stable way to run JS on real OS threads, not just processes (cluster) or the single event-loop thread
OpenSSL 1.1.1 minimum; Node defaults the max negotiated protocol to TLSv1.3 when the peer supports it
full ICU data bundled by default, replacing the old small-icu build -- Intl/String normalization work correctly for all locales out of the box
Apple Silicon (M1) support shipped Experimental at 16.0.0 GA, promoted to Tier 1 within the 16.x line and reflected as Tier 1 in BUILDING.md by 17.0.0
Windows-on-ARM64 has been Experimental since it first appeared in Node 12's platform table and had still not reached Tier 1 as of Node 26
arm64 GNU/Linux has been Tier 1 since the earliest tiered BUILDING.md tables (Node 6-8); believed Tier 1 already at the Node 4 reunification

LOW CONFIDENCE / from memory only, not independently verified this pass: an experimental node:quic module reappeared behind --experimental-quic around Node 23/24; Node has no HTTP/3 support in the fetch()/http client stack as of Node 26 researched here

os_support.windows: XP SP2+ / Server 2003+, x86 only via the 0.8.6+ .msi installer; no official x64 Windows build
os_support.macos: 10.5 (Leopard) and later, x64; built from source or an unofficial .pkg, no official installer
os_support.linux: any glibc Linux built from source; official prebuilt x86/x64 tarballs did not arrive until 0.10

limitations: no ES6/harmony syntax of any kind
V8 3.x -- no let/const/arrow functions even behind flags
no streams2 (original streams API only, notoriously hard to use correctly)

os_support.windows: XP+/Server 2003+, official x86 and (new) x64 installers
os_support.linux: glibc Linux, official prebuilt x86/x64 tarballs introduced

added: official prebuilt binary tarballs for Linux/SunOS
limitations: no native Promises without --harmony (added very late in this line's life)
cluster has no built-in sticky-session load balancing

os_support.windows: XP/Vista+ (last Node.js line released while XP/Vista were still officially supported targets)

limitations: async/await does not exist -- generators + a library like co are the state of the art
OpenSSL 1.0.1 -- no TLS 1.3, weak default cipher list by modern standards

os_support.windows: Vista and later (matching Node 0.12 at the io.js fork point)

added: forked from Node.js 0.10/0.12 core by contributors wanting a faster release cadence and current V8
more ES6 unflagged than Node 0.12 at the time
limitations: this was io.js, not Node.js -- a separate project/brand until the 2015-09-08 merger
lived under 3 months before io.js 2.0.0 superseded it
majors.notes: io.js major, not a Node.js major. Merged back into the Node.js Foundation as Node.js 4.0.0 on 2015-09-08; treat 'end_of_life' as that merger date in practice.

os_support.windows: Vista and later

added: V8 4.2 -- more ES6 (template literals, destructuring) available, some still behind --harmony
npm updated ahead of what Node 0.12 shipped
limitations: superseded by io.js 3.0.0 after about 3 months
majors.notes: io.js major. See note on major "1" about the 2015-09-08 merger into Node.js 4.0.0.

os_support.windows: Vista and later

added: OpenSSL 1.0.2 upgrade -- one of the changes carried directly into the Node 4 reunification
limitations: shortest-lived io.js major -- about 5 weeks before the Node.js 4.0.0 merger
majors.notes: io.js major, the last one; merged into Node.js 4.0.0 on 2015-09-08.

os_support.windows: XP/Vista/7/8/8.1/10, x86 and x64 (XP/Vista support continued past this release -- it was not dropped until Node 6.0.0)
os_support.macos: 10.7+ officially, Tier 1 x64
os_support.linux: glibc Linux x64/x86, arm64 promoted to full support at the io.js/Node.js reunification

added: reunification of io.js and Node.js under the Node.js Foundation
~half of ES2015 unflagged: let/const, classes, arrow functions, template literals, Map/Set
limitations: no worker_threads -- cluster/child_process are the only concurrency primitives
still officially supports Windows XP and Vista even though Microsoft had already end-of-lifed XP

os_support.windows: XP/Vista/7/8/8.1/10, x86/x64 (same floor as 4)

added: V8 4.6/4.8 -- more ES2015 (Proxy, Reflect, spread in function calls)
npm 3 as the default bundled version
limitations: never received LTS status -- 8-month lifespan, EOL before Node 6 even shipped its first LTS build

os_support.windows: Windows 7/Server 2008 R2 and later, x86/x64 (Windows XP and Vista support dropped in this release)
os_support.macos: 10.10+, Tier 1 x64 (formal BUILDING.md tier table introduced this release)
os_support.linux: Tier 1: kernel >=2.6.32, glibc >=2.12, x64/arm; arm64 kernel >=3.10; Tier 2: ppc64le, s390x, AIX >=7.1 TL04; FreeBSD >=10

added: official tiered BUILDING.md platform-support table introduced
Buffer(num) deprecation warnings begin (precursor to Buffer.alloc)
limitations: Windows XP and Vista officially dropped as of this release -- 4.x/5.x had still supported them

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2+, x86/x64 (same floor as 6)
os_support.linux: same tiers as 6: kernel >=2.6.32/glibc >=2.12 x64/arm, arm64 kernel >=3.10, ppc64le/s390x/AIX Tier 2

added: async/await landed behind --harmony-async-await at 7.0.0, unflagged in 7.6.0 -- the version most guides cite as "async/await support"
limitations: async/await needs a runtime flag until 7.6.0

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2+, x86/x64 (Tier 1, vs2015 or vs2017 toolchain)
os_support.macos: 10.10+ Tier 1 x64; 10.8-10.10 Experimental, no test coverage
os_support.linux: Tier 1: kernel >=2.6.32, glibc >=2.12, x64/arm; arm64 kernel >=3.10; Tier 2: ppc64le >=power8, s390x, AIX >=7.1 TL04; Experimental: musl (Alpine) x64

added: node:http2 added experimental behind --expose-http2 in 8.4.0, no flag needed from 8.8.0
ES modules usable behind --experimental-modules with .mjs from 8.5.0
limitations: ES modules require the --experimental-modules flag and .mjs extension
N-API is experimental -- no ABI stability guarantee yet

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2+, x86/x64

added: V8 6.2, tighter spec compliance (well-formed JSON.stringify, Promise.prototype.finally)

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2/2012 R2+, x86/x64, Tier 1
os_support.linux: Tier 1: kernel >=3.10, glibc >=2.17, x64; arm64 kernel >=4.5; armv7 kernel >=4.14; x86 downgraded to Experimental as of this release; Tier 2: ppc64le, s390x, AIX >=7.1 TL02

added: OpenSSL upgraded to 1.1.0 -- first Node line to do so
limitations: worker_threads still needs --experimental-worker and is experimental
no TLS 1.3 (OpenSSL 1.1.0 doesn't have it -- needs 1.1.1)
32-bit Linux (x86) downgraded from Tier 1 to Experimental this release

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2/2012 R2+, x86/x64, Tier 1
os_support.linux: same tiers as 10; FreeBSD bumped to >=11

added: worker_threads still experimental behind a flag

os_support.windows: Windows 7/2008 R2/2012 R2+, x86/x64 Tier 1; arm64 Windows appears for the first time, Experimental, >=Windows 10

added: worker_threads unflagged/stable (12.11.0) -- first stable true-parallelism primitive
TLS 1.3 supported and preferred by default when the peer supports it (OpenSSL 1.1.1)
ES modules usable without --experimental-modules from 12.17.0 (still prints an ExperimentalWarning)

os_support.windows: floor raised to Windows 8.1/2012 R2+ Tier 1; Windows 7 and plain Server 2012 (non-R2) demoted to Experimental -- Windows 7 support effectively dropped here
os_support.macos: floor raised to 10.13+ Tier 1
os_support.linux: same Tier 1/2 layout as 12; FreeBSD downgraded to Experimental as of Node 12

added: full ICU bundled by default (replacing small-icu) -- correct Intl/Unicode behavior for all locales without a custom build
limitations: Windows 7 / Server 2012 (non-R2) demoted to Experimental -- no longer an officially supported target
ES modules still experimental with warnings
worker_threads: no structured-clone support for every JS type yet

os_support.windows: Windows 8.1/2012 R2+ Tier 1 (unchanged from 13)

added: --experimental-modules flag requirement fully removed (import/export just work), though parts of ESM resolution remained experimental/warned
diagnostic report and AsyncLocalStorage marked stable
V8 8.1 -- optional chaining ?. and nullish coalescing ?? unflagged
npm 6 continued for most of this line's life (npm 7 was not backported by default)
limitations: dynamic import() / ESM loader hooks still experimental
top-level await not yet available outside ESM tricks
Windows 8.1/2012 R2 remains the floor -- unchanged from 13
no worker_threads structured-clone parity with the main thread for all types

os_support.windows: Windows 8.1/2012 R2+ Tier 1 (no bump yet -- that happens at 16)
os_support.macos: 10.13+ Tier 1, x64 only -- no arm64 row at all (pre-Apple-Silicon)

added: npm 7 bundled by default -- workspaces, automatic peer-dependency installation, and a new lockfile format
limitations: still no fetch or global Web Streams
no Apple Silicon support at all -- Mac binaries are x64-only and must run under Rosetta on M1 hardware

os_support.windows: floor raised to Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1; Windows 8.1/2012 R2 demoted to Experimental
os_support.macos: x64 Tier 1 >=10.15; arm64 (Apple Silicon) appears for the first time, Experimental, >=11 -- promoted to Tier 1 later within the 16.x line
os_support.linux: same Tier 1/2 layout as prior majors

added: Apple Silicon (arm64 macOS) support, experimental at GA and promoted to Tier 1 during the 16.x LTS life
corepack shipped experimental (16.9.0), bundling pnpm/yarn shims behind `corepack enable`
limitations: Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2 demoted to Experimental -- Windows 10+ is now the supported floor
Apple Silicon builds are Experimental at the initial 16.0.0 release
corepack itself is experimental and opt-in via `corepack enable`

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1 (unchanged from 16)
os_support.macos: arm64 promoted to Tier 1 (>=11); x64 Tier 1 >=10.15

added: OpenSSL 3.0 becomes the default (up from 1.1.1) -- new provider architecture
limitations: OpenSSL 3.0 breaks some legacy crypto usage (certain algorithms/PBKDF configs) unless --openssl-legacy-provider is passed

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1
os_support.macos: x64 Tier 1 >=10.15; arm64 Tier 1 >=11 (floors unchanged from 17)

added: global fetch API available without a flag but marked experimental (undici-based)
Web Streams globals (ReadableStream, WritableStream, TransformStream) unflagged
limitations: fetch is experimental and prints a warning; no HTTP proxy support in fetch
OpenSSL 3 legacy-provider friction persists for some crypto users
Intel Mac floor (10.15) had not risen to match Apple Silicon's 11 yet

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1
os_support.macos: x64 Tier 1 >=10.15; arm64 Tier 1 >=11 (unchanged from 18)

added: fetch keep-alive behavior improvements via undici

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1
os_support.macos: floor raised to >=11.0 Tier 1 for BOTH x64 and arm64 (10.15 dropped)

limitations: permission model experimental and incomplete (not all subsystems honor it)
macOS 10.15 (Catalina) support dropped -- 11+ required from here on

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1
os_support.macos: >=11.0 Tier 1 for x64 and arm64 (unchanged from 20)

added: import attributes (`with { type: "json" }`) replace the older import-assertions syntax for JSON modules
limitations: no require(esm) yet -- CommonJS still cannot require() a synchronous ESM-only package

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1 (x86/WoW64 rows still nominally present in BUILDING.md at GA, but on the way out)
os_support.macos: >=11.0 Tier 1 for x64 and arm64
os_support.linux: same Tier 1/2 layout as prior majors, plus loong64 added as Experimental

added: require(esm): experimental support for require()-ing a synchronous ES module
--experimental-strip-types added in 22.6.0 -- run .ts files directly by stripping type annotations, no type-checking
--experimental-transform-types added in 22.7.0 for constructs stripping can't handle (enums, namespaces, parameter properties)
limitations: require(esm) still needed a flag at GA (unflagged later, in 22.12.0)
TypeScript support is type-stripping only, never type-checking, and only through experimental flags at this point
32-bit Windows support was still nominally present but was dropped two majors later, at 24

os_support.windows: Windows 10/Server 2016+ Tier 1 (still lists x86/WoW64)
os_support.macos: >=11.0 Tier 1 for x64 and arm64

added: require(esm) and --experimental-strip-types both unflagged/stable in 23.6.0 -- Node natively runs .ts files with no CLI flag needed
limitations: enums, namespaces, and experimental decorators still need the separate --experimental-transform-types flag

os_support.windows: floor unchanged at Windows 10/Server 2016+, but 32-bit Windows (x86/WoW64) is REMOVED entirely -- Windows x64 (Tier 1) and arm64 (Tier 2) only from here on
os_support.macos: floor raised sharply to >=13.5 (Ventura, a later patch) for both x64 and arm64 -- 11.0-13.4 dropped
os_support.linux: x64/arm64 Tier 1 unchanged; 32-bit ARM (armv7) downgraded from Tier 1 to Experimental

added: TypeScript type stripping is the default for .ts files, no flag needed (still no type-checking)
limitations: 32-bit Windows (x86) is no longer an officially supported platform at all
macOS 11-13.4 no longer supported -- 13.5 is the new floor, a much bigger jump than prior majors
type stripping still can't type-check or handle enums/namespaces without --experimental-transform-types

os_support.windows: Windows x64 Tier 1 / arm64 Tier 2 only (unchanged from 24)
os_support.macos: >=13.5 Tier 1 for x64 and arm64 (unchanged from 24)
os_support.linux: same as 24, plus OpenHarmony arm64 added as an Experimental target

limitations: corepack is no longer distributed with Node.js by default -- `npm install -g corepack` (or a package manager's own installer) is now required; this ends the bundling era that ran from 14.19/16.9 through 24.x and will break CI/Docker images that assumed `corepack enable` just worked
majors.notes: Corepack removal confirmed via the nodejs/corepack GitHub issue tracker and Socket.dev coverage of the TSC vote; the platform table itself is high confidence (fetched directly from BUILDING.md at the v25.0.0 tag).

os_support.windows: Windows x64 Tier 1 / arm64 Tier 2 only (unchanged from 24-25)
os_support.macos: >=13.5 Tier 1 for x64 and arm64 (unchanged from 24-25)
os_support.linux: x64/arm64 Tier 1 unchanged; ppc64le and AIX minimum raised from Power8 to Power9; s390x minimum raised to z14; riscv64 added as a new Experimental target alongside loong64

added: Temporal API enabled by default -- a modern date/time API intended to replace much of the ad hoc Date/moment.js/date-fns usage
limitations: http.Server.prototype.writeHeader() and the legacy internal _stream_* modules (_stream_wrap, _stream_readable, _stream_writable, _stream_duplex, _stream_transform, _stream_passthrough) are removed entirely -- old shims/polyfills touching them break
module.register() is now runtime-deprecated ahead of eventual removal
older POWER8 and pre-z14 mainframe hardware can no longer run official builds -- the AIX/ppc64/s390x floors were raised
as of this research date (2026-09-17) Node 26 is still Current-only -- it does not enter LTS until 2026-10-28, so treating it as production-stable ahead of that date is premature
majors.notes: Newest major in scope, only ~4.5 months old at research time. Platform table is high confidence (fetched directly from BUILDING.md at the v26.0.0 tag); the feature/deprecation list comes from the nodejs.org v26.0.0 blog post (a primary source, but not yet cross-checked against a full changelog or field experience the way older majors could be).
